context: Select and write the correct answer for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: Integrated rate law equation for a zero order reaction is \(-\)
solution:
**(A)** \(kt = [A]_0 - [A]_t\)

For a zero order reaction the rate does not depend on concentration:

\(-\dfrac{d[A]}{dt} = k\)

Separating and integrating from \([A]_0\) at \(t = 0\) to \([A]_t\) at time \(t\),

\([A]_0 - [A]_t = kt\)

\(\therefore kt = [A]_0 - [A]_t\)

Option (C) has the two concentrations the wrong way round, which would make \(k\) negative — impossible for a rate constant. Options (B) and (D) contain a logarithm, and a logarithmic form belongs to a **first order** reaction, not a zero order one.

context: Select and write the correct answer for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: The spin only magnetic moment of \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) ion is ____.
solution:
**(B)** 4.899 BM

**Step 1 — the configuration.** Iron has \(Z = 26\), so \(\mathrm{Fe: [Ar]\,3d^{6}4s^{2}}\). To form \(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}\) the two \(4s\) electrons are removed first:

\(\mathrm{Fe^{2+}: [Ar]\ 3d^{6}}\)

**Step 2 — the unpaired electrons.** Six electrons in five \(d\) orbitals: by Hund's rule the first five go in singly and the sixth pairs up with one of them. That leaves

\(n = 4\) unpaired electrons

**Step 3 — the spin-only formula.**

\(\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{4 \times 6} = \sqrt{24}\)

\(\therefore \mu = 4.899\ \mathrm{BM}\)

The step that catches people out is removing the \(4s\) electrons before the \(3d\) ones. Taking \(3d^{4}4s^{2}\) instead would give \(n = 4\) here by coincidence, but it is wrong in general.

context: Select and write the correct answer for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: The relation between radius of sphere and edge length in simple cubic lattice is ____.
solution:
**(C)** \(r = \dfrac{a}{2}\)

In a **simple cubic** lattice the particles sit only at the eight corners, and neighbouring particles touch **along the edge** of the cube.

Along one edge of length \(a\) lie one radius from the particle at each end:

\(r + r = a\)

\(2r = a\)

\(\therefore r = \dfrac{a}{2}\)

The other options belong to the other cubic systems. \(\sqrt{3}\,a = 4r\) is body centred cubic, where contact is along the body diagonal, and \(\sqrt{2}\,a = 4r\) is face centred cubic, where contact is along the face diagonal.

context: Select and write the correct answer for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: The monomer used in the preparation of thermocol is ____.
solution:
**(D)** styrene

Thermocol is **expanded polystyrene**. Polystyrene is made by the addition polymerisation of styrene, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5{-}CH{=}CH_2}\):

\(n\,\mathrm{C_6H_5CH{=}CH_2 \longrightarrow (\!-CH_2{-}CH(C_6H_5)-\!)_n}\)

To make thermocol the polymer beads are expanded with a blowing agent so that the finished material is mostly trapped air, which is what makes it so light and such a good insulator.

The other monomers give different polymers: vinyl chloride gives PVC, and butadiene with acrylonitrile gives the synthetic rubber Buna-N.

context: Select and write the correct answer for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: The pH of 0.01 M solution of HCl is \(-\)
solution:
**(C)** 2

HCl is a strong acid, so it is completely ionised and every mole gives one mole of \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\):

\([\mathrm{H^{+}}] = 0.01 = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{M}\)

\(\mathrm{pH} = -\log[\mathrm{H^{+}}] = -\log(10^{-2})\)

\(\therefore \mathrm{pH} = 2\)

context: Select and write the correct answer for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: Which of the following \(\alpha\)-amino acids do not contain chiral centre?
solution:
**(D)** glycine

An \(\alpha\)-amino acid has the general structure \(\mathrm{H_2N{-}CHR{-}COOH}\). The \(\alpha\)-carbon carries four groups: \(\mathrm{{-}NH_2}\), \(\mathrm{{-}COOH}\), \(\mathrm{{-}H}\) and the side chain R. It is chiral provided all four are different.

**Glycine** is the one amino acid in which \(\mathrm{R = H}\):

\(\mathrm{H_2N{-}CH_2{-}COOH}\)

So the \(\alpha\)-carbon carries **two hydrogen atoms**. Two of its four groups are identical, the molecule has a plane of symmetry, and there is no chiral centre.

Alanine \((\mathrm{R = CH_3})\), valine and leucine all have distinct carbon side chains, so all three are chiral and optically active.

\(\therefore\) glycine is the only achiral \(\alpha\)-amino acid, and it is the simplest one.

context: Select and write the correct answer for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: Among the following benzylic halide is ____. (The four options are drawn structures — see the figure.)

options.label: A
options.text: a benzene ring with X bonded directly to a ring carbon

options.label: B
options.text: a benzene ring with a \(\mathrm{{-}CH_2X}\) group on it

options.label: C
options.text: a cyclohexene ring with X on the carbon next to the double bond

options.label: D
options.text: a benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{{-}CH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{{-}X}\) on adjacent ring carbons

solution:
**(B)** the benzene ring carrying a \(\mathrm{{-}CH_2X}\) group

A **benzylic halide** is one in which the halogen is attached to an \(sp^{3}\) carbon that is itself bonded directly to a benzene ring. That \(sp^{3}\) carbon is the benzylic position.

In option (B) the halogen sits on the \(\mathrm{{-}CH_2{-}}\) group attached to the ring, which is exactly that arrangement.

The others are different classes:

- **(A)** has the halogen bonded directly to a ring carbon, which is \(sp^{2}\). That is an **aryl** halide, and its \(\mathrm{C{-}X}\) bond has partial double bond character, making it very unreactive to substitution.
- **(C)** has the halogen on the carbon adjacent to a \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) in a non-aromatic ring — an **allylic** halide.
- **(D)** again has the halogen directly on the ring, so it too is an aryl halide; the methyl group elsewhere on the ring does not change that.

The distinction matters because benzylic and allylic halides react readily by \(S_N1\), their carbocations being resonance stabilised, while aryl halides do neither.

context: Select and write the correct answer for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: Neutral complex in the following is _____
solution:
**(A)** \(\mathrm{[Co(NO_2)_3(NH_3)_3]}\)

A **neutral complex** carries no charge on the coordination sphere, so it needs no counter ion at all — nothing is written outside the square brackets.

Check option (A): cobalt is \(+3\), the three nitrite ligands give \(3 \times (-1) = -3\) and the three ammonia ligands are neutral.

\((+3) + (-3) + 0 = 0\)

The complex is neutral, and the formula shows nothing outside the brackets. This is the answer.

The others all fail:

- **(B)** has \(\mathrm{Cl}\) written outside the brackets, so the complex ion is a cation balanced by a chloride.
- **(C)** has three sodium ions outside, so the complex is an anion.
- **(D)** carries an explicit \(3-\) charge.

context: Select and write the correct answer for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: The reaction used to convert toluene to benzaldehyde is known as :
solution:
**(A)** Etard's reaction

Toluene is oxidised to benzaldehyde by chromyl chloride, \(\mathrm{CrO_2Cl_2}\), in carbon disulfide or carbon tetrachloride:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_3 \xrightarrow{CrO_2Cl_2 / CS_2} C_6H_5CH(OCrOHCl_2)_2 \xrightarrow{H_3O^{+}} C_6H_5CHO}\)

The methyl group first forms a brown **chromium complex**, which is isolated and then hydrolysed. That intermediate is the whole point of the method: it protects the product from being oxidised further to benzoic acid, which is what an ordinary oxidising agent would do.

The others do something different. The **Gatterman-Koch** reaction makes benzaldehyde from **benzene** with CO and HCl, not from toluene. **Friedel-Crafts** attaches an alkyl or acyl group to a ring. The **Swartz** reaction converts an alkyl chloride to an alkyl fluoride and involves no ring at all.

context: Select and write the correct answer for the following multiple choice type of questions :
stem: A better reagent to convert primary alcohol to aldehyde is ____.
solution:
**(B)** pyridinium chlorochromate

The difficulty in this conversion is **stopping at the aldehyde**. A primary alcohol is oxidised first to the aldehyde and then, very readily, on to the carboxylic acid. So the question is not which reagent oxidises, but which stops.

**Pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC)** is used in the **anhydrous** solvent dichloromethane. Further oxidation of an aldehyde to an acid needs water, because it proceeds through the hydrate; with no water present the reaction halts at the aldehyde:

\(\mathrm{RCH_2OH \xrightarrow[CH_2Cl_2]{PCC} RCHO}\)

The word **better** in the question is pointing at exactly this.

Potassium permanganate and potassium dichromate are strong oxidising agents used in aqueous acid, so both carry straight on to the carboxylic acid. Chromic anhydride \((\mathrm{CrO_3})\) in aqueous acid does the same.

subtopic: Uses and Environmental Effects of Polyhalogen Compounds
stem: Write the name of insecticide which is effectively used instead of DDT.
solution:
**Gammexane**, the \(\gamma\) isomer of benzene hexachloride, also called **lindane** or BHC.

It is used in place of DDT because it is effective at lower doses and degrades somewhat faster, so it accumulates less in the food chain. DDT itself is now banned or severely restricted in most countries because it is extremely persistent and concentrates up the food chain, thinning the eggshells of birds of prey.

stem: Write the name of hydrocarbon formed when methyl magnesium iodide is treated with ammonia.
solution:
The hydrocarbon is **methane**, \(\mathrm{CH_4}\).

A Grignard reagent carries a strongly polarised \(\mathrm{C{-}Mg}\) bond in which the carbon is effectively a **carbanion**, so it behaves as a very powerful base. It abstracts a proton from any compound with an acidic hydrogen — water, alcohols, amines or ammonia:

\(\mathrm{CH_3MgI + NH_3 \longrightarrow CH_4\uparrow + Mg(NH_2)I}\)

The methyl group leaves as methane.

This is also why a Grignard reagent must be prepared and used in scrupulously **dry** conditions: any source of an acidic hydrogen destroys it before it can do useful work.

stem:
Calculate the standard potential of the following cell at 25°C :

\(\mathrm{Zn_{(s)} \mid Zn^{2+}(0.08\,M) \parallel Cr^{3+}(0.1\,M) \mid Cr_{(s)}}\)

\(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Zn}} = -0.76\ \mathrm{V}\), \(E^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cr}} = -0.74\ \mathrm{V}\)
solution:
In the cell notation the **anode** is on the left and the **cathode** on the right, so zinc is oxidised and chromium is reduced.

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cathode}} - E^{\circ}_{\text{anode}}\)

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = (-0.74) - (-0.76)\)

\(E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = -0.74 + 0.76\)

\(\therefore E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} = +0.02\ \mathrm{V}\)

The value is positive, so the cell reaction

\(\mathrm{3Zn + 2Cr^{3+} \longrightarrow 3Zn^{2+} + 2Cr}\)

is spontaneous, though only barely — the two electrodes are very close in the electrochemical series.

**On the concentrations.** The question asks for the **standard** potential, which is defined at 1 M for every species, so the given 0.08 M and 0.1 M do not enter this calculation. They would be needed only for the actual cell potential under those conditions, through the Nernst equation with \(n = 6\).

stem: Write the IUPAC name of \(\mathrm{Na_3[AlF_6]}\).
solution:
Name the cation first, then the complex anion.

The ligands are six fluorides, named **hexafluorido** (older texts: hexafluoro).

Oxidation state of aluminium: \(x + 6(-1) = -3\), so \(x = +3\).

Because the complex ion is an **anion**, the metal takes the *-ate* suffix, and for aluminium that is aluminate.

\(\therefore\) the IUPAC name is **sodium hexafluoridoaluminate(III)**.

The compound is cryolite, used as the molten solvent for alumina in the electrolytic extraction of aluminium.

subtopic: Position in the Periodic Table and Electronic Configuration
stem: Write the electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) ion. (Atomic number of zinc is 30).
solution:
Zinc has \(Z = 30\), so the neutral atom is

\(\mathrm{Zn: [Ar]\ 3d^{10}\ 4s^{2}}\)

To form \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\), two electrons are removed. For a transition metal the **\(4s\) electrons are always removed first**, even though \(4s\) is filled before \(3d\):

\(\therefore \mathrm{Zn^{2+}: [Ar]\ 3d^{10}}\)

or written out in full, \(\mathrm{1s^{2}2s^{2}2p^{6}3s^{2}3p^{6}3d^{10}}\).

The \(3d\) subshell is completely filled, which is why \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) has no unpaired electrons: it is diamagnetic and its compounds are colourless.

stem: Write the IUPAC name of amine formed when acetamide undergoes Hofmann bromamide degradation.
solution:
In **Hofmann bromamide degradation** an amide is treated with bromine and alkali, and the product is a primary amine with **one carbon atom fewer** than the amide.

Acetamide, \(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2}\), has two carbons, so the amine has one:

\(\mathrm{CH_3CONH_2 + Br_2 + 4NaOH \longrightarrow CH_3NH_2 + Na_2CO_3 + 2NaBr + 2H_2O}\)

The product is \(\mathrm{CH_3NH_2}\).

\(\therefore\) its IUPAC name is **methanamine** (common name methylamine).

The carbonyl carbon is lost as carbonate. This is the feature that distinguishes the reaction from simple reduction of the amide, which keeps both carbons and would give ethanamine instead.

stem: Write the condition for spontaneity of reaction with respect to entropy.
solution:
A process is spontaneous when the **total entropy of the system and its surroundings increases**:

\(\Delta S_{\text{total}} = \Delta S_{\text{system}} + \Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} > 0\)

The three cases are:

- \(\Delta S_{\text{total}} > 0\) — the process is **spontaneous**
- \(\Delta S_{\text{total}} = 0\) — the system is at **equilibrium**
- \(\Delta S_{\text{total}} < 0\) — the process is **non-spontaneous**, and the reverse process is spontaneous

The word **total** is essential. The entropy of the system alone may perfectly well decrease in a spontaneous process, as it does when water freezes, provided the surroundings gain more entropy than the system loses.

stem: Write the relation between van't Hoff factor and degree of dissociation of an electrolyte.
solution:
If one formula unit of an electrolyte dissociates into \(n\) ions and \(\alpha\) is its degree of dissociation, then the van't Hoff factor is

\(i = 1 + (n - 1)\alpha\)

Rearranged to give the degree of dissociation,

\(\therefore \alpha = \dfrac{i - 1}{n - 1}\)

**Where it comes from.** Starting with 1 mole, a fraction \(\alpha\) dissociates, leaving \((1 - \alpha)\) undissociated and producing \(n\alpha\) ions. The total number of particles is

\((1 - \alpha) + n\alpha = 1 + (n-1)\alpha\)

and \(i\) is by definition the ratio of the observed number of particles to the number expected without dissociation, which is 1.

So \(i > 1\) indicates dissociation, and \(i < 1\) indicates association, as happens with a carboxylic acid dimerising in benzene.

stem:
The normal boiling point of ethyl acetate is 77.06 °C. A solution of 50 g of non-volatile solute in 150 g ethyl acetate boils at 82.60 °C. Calculate molar mass of solute.

\([K_b = 2.77\ \mathrm{{}^{\circ}C\ kg\ mol^{-1}}]\)
solution:
**Step 1 — the elevation in boiling point.**

\(\Delta T_b = 82.60 - 77.06 = 5.54\ \mathrm{{}^{\circ}C}\)

**Step 2 — the working formula.** From \(\Delta T_b = K_b m\) with \(m = \dfrac{1000\,w_2}{M_2 w_1}\),

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1000\,K_b\,w_2}{\Delta T_b \, w_1}\)

where \(w_2\) is the mass of solute and \(w_1\) the mass of solvent, both in grams.

**Step 3 — substitute.** \(w_2 = 50\ \mathrm{g}\), \(w_1 = 150\ \mathrm{g}\), \(K_b = 2.77\).

\(M_2 = \dfrac{1000 \times 2.77 \times 50}{5.54 \times 150}\)

\(M_2 = \dfrac{138500}{831}\)

\(\therefore M_2 = 166.7\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

stem:
Deduce first law of thermodynamics for :

(a) isothermal process

(b) isochoric process
solution:
The general statement is

\(\Delta U = Q + W\)

**(a) Isothermal process.** The temperature is constant. For an **ideal gas** the internal energy depends only on temperature, so

\(\Delta U = 0\)

Substituting,

\(0 = Q + W\)

\(\therefore Q = -W\)

All the heat absorbed by the system is converted into work done by it, and vice versa. This is why an isothermal expansion needs heat to be supplied continuously to keep the temperature from falling.

**(b) Isochoric process.** The volume is constant, so \(\Delta V = 0\) and no pressure-volume work is done:

\(W = -P\Delta V = 0\)

\(\therefore \Delta U = Q_V\)

All the heat supplied goes into raising the internal energy. This is the basis of the bomb calorimeter, which is rigid and therefore measures \(\Delta U\) directly rather than \(\Delta H\).

stem:
Complete the following equations :

(i) \(\mathrm{XeF_2 + H_2O \longrightarrow\ ?}\)

(ii) \(\mathrm{Xe + F_2 \xrightarrow[\text{Low temperature}]{\text{Electric discharge}}\ ?}\)
solution:
**(i) Hydrolysis of xenon difluoride.** \(\mathrm{XeF_2}\) is hydrolysed by water, and the xenon is reduced to the free element:

\(\mathrm{2XeF_2 + 2H_2O \longrightarrow 2Xe + 4HF + O_2}\)

The products are **xenon, hydrogen fluoride and oxygen**. Note that this is a redox reaction, not a simple exchange: xenon goes from \(+2\) to 0 while the oxygen of water goes from \(-2\) to 0.

**(ii) Direct combination.** Xenon and fluorine combine directly, and the ratio of the two decides which fluoride is formed. Under electric discharge at low temperature, with xenon in excess, the product is the **difluoride**:

\(\mathrm{Xe + F_2 \xrightarrow[\text{low temp.}]{\text{electric discharge}} XeF_2}\)

With a larger excess of fluorine and more forcing conditions the same reaction gives \(\mathrm{XeF_4}\) at a 1:5 ratio and 873 K, and \(\mathrm{XeF_6}\) at 1:20 and high pressure.

stem: Differentiate between ionic crystals and covalent crystals.
solution:
| Ionic crystals | Covalent crystals |
|---|---|
| Constituent particles are **cations and anions**. | Constituent particles are **atoms**. |
| Held together by strong **electrostatic** forces of attraction. | Held together by **covalent bonds** forming a continuous network. |
| Hard and brittle — they shatter when a layer is displaced, because like charges come opposite each other. | Very hard, and not brittle in the same way; some, like graphite, are soft because of weak forces BETWEEN layers. |
| High melting points, typically 800 to 1000 °C. | Extremely high melting points, often above 2000 °C. |
| **Non-conductors in the solid state** but good conductors when molten or dissolved, since the ions become free to move. | **Non-conductors** in every state, since there are no free ions. Graphite is the exception, having delocalised electrons between its layers. |
| Generally **soluble** in polar solvents such as water. | **Insoluble** in all ordinary solvents. |
| Examples: NaCl, KCl, \(\mathrm{CaF_2}\), ZnS. | Examples: diamond, silicon carbide, quartz \((\mathrm{SiO_2})\), graphite. |

The underlying difference is that an ionic crystal is a lattice of discrete charged particles, while a covalent crystal is effectively **one giant molecule** — every atom is bonded to its neighbours by directional covalent bonds running through the whole solid. That is why melting one means breaking chemical bonds rather than merely overcoming electrostatic attraction.

stem:
What is the mass of Cu metal produced at the cathode during the passage of 5 ampere of current through \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\) solution for 100 minutes?

[Molar mass of Cu = \(63.5\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)]
solution:
**Step 1 — charge passed.** Time must be in seconds:

\(t = 100 \times 60 = 6000\ \mathrm{s}\)

\(Q = I \times t = 5 \times 6000 = 30000\ \mathrm{C}\)

**Step 2 — electrons per copper atom.** The cathode reaction is

\(\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^{-} \longrightarrow Cu}\)

so 2 moles of electrons are needed per mole of copper, that is

\(2 \times 96500 = 193000\ \mathrm{C\ mol^{-1}}\)

**Step 3 — moles of copper deposited.**

\(n = \dfrac{30000}{193000} = 0.1554\ \mathrm{mol}\)

**Step 4 — mass.**

\(m = n \times M = 0.1554 \times 63.5\)

\(\therefore m = 9.87\ \mathrm{g}\)

The step most often missed is the factor of 2 for the electrons. Using 96500 instead of 193000 would double the answer.

stem: Define Buffer solution. Write the Henderson Hasselbalch equation for acidic buffer.
solution:
**Definition.** A **buffer solution** is one that resists a change in its pH when a small amount of a strong acid or a strong base is added to it, or when it is diluted.

An **acidic buffer** is a mixture of a weak acid and its salt with a strong base — for example acetic acid with sodium acetate. A **basic buffer** is a weak base with its salt with a strong acid, such as ammonia with ammonium chloride.

**Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer.**

\(\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a + \log\dfrac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}\)

Two consequences worth noting. When the salt and acid concentrations are equal the logarithm is zero, so \(\mathrm{pH} = \mathrm{p}K_a\) — that is the point of maximum buffer capacity. And since only the **ratio** appears, diluting the buffer changes both concentrations equally and leaves the pH unaltered.

stem: Write two principles of green chemistry.
solution:
**1. Prevention of waste.** It is better to prevent waste from being formed in the first place than to treat or clean it up after it has been produced. Waste that is never made needs no disposal and carries no cost.

**2. Atom economy.** A synthetic route should be designed so that the **maximum possible proportion of the atoms of the reactants** ends up in the desired product. An addition reaction has 100% atom economy by construction, whereas a substitution or elimination necessarily discards part of the starting material.

(Other accepted principles: use of safer solvents and auxiliaries; design for energy efficiency, running reactions at ambient temperature and pressure; use of renewable feedstocks; catalysis in preference to stoichiometric reagents; designing chemicals that degrade after use; and real-time analysis to prevent pollution.)

stem: Write the preparation of Nylon-6 polymer and its two uses.
solution:
**Preparation.** Nylon-6 is made from a **single** monomer, caprolactam, a cyclic amide containing six carbon atoms — which is where the name comes from.

Heating caprolactam to about 533 K with a trace of water opens the ring and polymerises it:

\(n\,\mathrm{[(CH_2)_5CONH]} \xrightarrow[533\ K]{H_2O} \mathrm{[{-}NH{-}(CH_2)_5{-}CO{-}]}_n\)

The water initiates the ring opening; the polymer then grows by successive addition of further caprolactam units. The product is a polyamide, so the chains are held to one another by hydrogen bonds between neighbouring amide groups.

**Two uses.**

1. **Tyre cord and industrial ropes**, where its high tensile strength and resistance to abrasion are needed.
2. **Textile fibre** for fabrics, and for making fishing nets and bristles.

Note the contrast with Nylon 6,6, which needs **two** monomers and is made by condensation with loss of water.

stem:
Define :

(a) Pyrometallurgy.

(b) Roasting.
solution:
**(a) Pyrometallurgy.** The extraction of a metal from its ore by processes carried out at **high temperature**, in which the metal oxide is reduced by a suitable reducing agent such as carbon, carbon monoxide or another metal.

The word comes from the Greek *pyro*, meaning fire. The extraction of iron in a blast furnace is the standard example:

\(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3 + 3CO \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2Fe + 3CO_2}\)

**(b) Roasting.** The process of heating a **sulfide** ore strongly **in the presence of excess air**, below its melting point, so that the sulfide is converted to the oxide:

\(\mathrm{2ZnS + 3O_2 \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2ZnO + 2SO_2}\)

Roasting also drives off volatile impurities of arsenic and antimony as their oxides.

It should not be confused with **calcination**, which is the heating of a carbonate ore in the **absence or limited supply** of air, to give the oxide and carbon dioxide.

subtopic: Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions of Alkyl Halides
stem: Write salient features of \(S_N1\) mechanism.
solution:
**Salient features of the \(S_N1\) mechanism.**

1. **It occurs in two steps.** The first is the slow, rate determining ionisation of the alkyl halide to a carbocation; the second is the fast attack of the nucleophile on that carbocation.

\(\mathrm{R{-}X \xrightarrow{slow} R^{+} + X^{-}}\)

\(\mathrm{R^{+} + Nu^{-} \xrightarrow{fast} R{-}Nu}\)

2. **The kinetics are first order.** Only the halide appears in the rate determining step, so

\(\text{rate} = k[\mathrm{RX}]\)

The concentration of the nucleophile does not affect the rate. This is what the 1 in \(S_N1\) denotes — unimolecular.

3. **A carbocation is formed as an intermediate**, and the rate therefore follows carbocation stability:

tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl

So \(S_N1\) is the mechanism of **tertiary** halides, and also of allylic and benzylic ones whose cations are resonance stabilised.

4. **The product is racemised.** The carbocation is planar and \(sp^{2}\) hybridised, so the nucleophile can attack either face with equal ease. An optically pure chiral halide therefore gives a nearly 50:50 mixture of both enantiomers.

5. **Polar protic solvents favour it**, since they solvate and stabilise the carbocation and the leaving halide ion.

6. **Rearrangement can occur** if a hydride or alkyl shift converts the carbocation into a more stable one before the nucleophile arrives.

stem: What is the denaturation of proteins? Write the name of only pyrimidine base in RNA.
solution:
**Denaturation of proteins.** The loss of the **secondary and tertiary structure** of a protein, caused by heat, change of pH, addition of heavy metal salts, alcohol or urea, which destroys its biological activity.

The hydrogen bonds, disulfide bridges and other weak interactions that hold the chain in its folded shape are broken, and the globular protein uncoils into an irregular strand. The **primary structure**, the sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds, is **not** affected, since that requires covalent bonds to break.

The everyday example is boiling an egg: the soluble globular albumin coagulates into an insoluble white solid, and the change cannot be reversed by cooling.

**Pyrimidine bases in RNA.** RNA contains two pyrimidine bases, cytosine and **uracil**.

The base that is present in RNA and **not** in DNA is **uracil**, which replaces the thymine found in DNA.

stem:
Write the reaction when ethylamine is treated with :

(a) excess of ethyl bromide

(b) Hinsberg's reagent
solution:
**(a) Excess of ethyl bromide — exhaustive alkylation.**

Ethylamine is a nucleophile and attacks ethyl bromide in an \(S_N2\) substitution. The product is itself an amine and is at least as nucleophilic, so with the halide in excess the alkylation does not stop:

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2 \xrightarrow{C_2H_5Br} (C_2H_5)_2NH \xrightarrow{C_2H_5Br} (C_2H_5)_3N \xrightarrow{C_2H_5Br} (C_2H_5)_4N^{+}Br^{-}}\)

The final product with **excess** ethyl bromide is **tetraethylammonium bromide**, a quaternary ammonium salt.

This inability to stop at one stage is exactly why direct alkylation is a poor preparative route to a pure secondary or tertiary amine — the Gabriel synthesis is used instead.

**(b) Hinsberg's reagent — benzenesulfonyl chloride.**

\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2 + C_6H_5SO_2Cl \longrightarrow C_6H_5SO_2NH{-}C_2H_5 + HCl}\)

The product is N-ethylbenzenesulfonamide.

Because ethylamine is **primary**, the product still carries one hydrogen on nitrogen. That hydrogen is acidic, the adjacent sulfonyl group withdrawing electron density, so the sulfonamide **dissolves in aqueous alkali**:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5SO_2NH{-}C_2H_5 + NaOH \longrightarrow C_6H_5SO_2N^{-}(Na^{+}){-}C_2H_5 + H_2O}\)

This solubility is the test. A secondary amine gives a sulfonamide with no \(\mathrm{N{-}H}\) and so an alkali-insoluble product, and a tertiary amine does not react at all.

stem:
Construct a cell using standard hydrogen electrode and zinc electrode. Write its cell reaction and cell representation.

Calculate cell potential of a cell with \(0.01\ \mathrm{M}\ \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) ions. Standard potential of a cell is \(+0.76\) V.
solution:
**Which electrode is the anode?** The standard potential of zinc is \(-0.76\ \mathrm{V}\) and that of the hydrogen electrode is 0 by definition. Zinc is the stronger reducing agent, so zinc is oxidised and is the **anode**; the hydrogen electrode is the **cathode**.

**Cell reactions.**

At the anode (oxidation): \(\mathrm{Zn_{(s)} \longrightarrow Zn^{2+}_{(aq)} + 2e^{-}}\)

At the cathode (reduction): \(\mathrm{2H^{+}_{(aq)} + 2e^{-} \longrightarrow H_{2(g)}}\)

Overall: \(\mathrm{Zn_{(s)} + 2H^{+}_{(aq)} \longrightarrow Zn^{2+}_{(aq)} + H_{2(g)}}\)

**Cell representation.** Anode on the left, cathode on the right:

\(\mathrm{Zn_{(s)} \mid Zn^{2+}_{(aq)} \parallel H^{+}_{(aq)}\,(1\ M) \mid H_{2(g)}\,(1\ bar) \mid Pt}\)

**Cell potential with \(0.01\ \mathrm{M}\ \mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\).** Apply the Nernst equation with \(n = 2\). The hydrogen electrode is at standard conditions, so only the zinc ion concentration enters:

\(E_{\text{cell}} = E^{\circ}_{\text{cell}} - \dfrac{0.0592}{n}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\mathrm{H^{+}}]^{2}}\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0.76 - \dfrac{0.0592}{2}\log(0.01)\)

\(\log(0.01) = -2\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0.76 - 0.0296 \times (-2)\)

\(E_{\text{cell}} = 0.76 + 0.0592\)

\(\therefore E_{\text{cell}} = 0.819\ \mathrm{V}\)

The potential is **higher** than the standard value, which is what should be expected: the product \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) is below 1 M, so by Le Chatelier's principle the forward reaction is more favoured.

subtopic: Vapour Pressure of Solutions of Liquids in Liquids
stem:
State Henry's Law.

Write four conditions for ideal solutions.
solution:
**Henry's law.** The solubility of a gas in a liquid at a given temperature is **directly proportional to the pressure of the gas** above the liquid.

\(S = K_H \times P\)

where \(S\) is the solubility, \(P\) the partial pressure of the gas and \(K_H\) Henry's law constant, which has the unit \(\mathrm{mol\ L^{-1}\ bar^{-1}}\).

The law holds only for a gas that does not react with the solvent, at moderate pressure, and it fails at high pressure or when the gas dissociates in solution.

**Four conditions for an ideal solution.**

1. It **obeys Raoult's law** over the whole range of composition, for each component and at all temperatures:

\(p_1 = p_1^{\circ}x_1\) and \(p_2 = p_2^{\circ}x_2\)

2. The **enthalpy of mixing is zero**, \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H = 0\) — no heat is absorbed or evolved on mixing.

3. The **volume of mixing is zero**, \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}V = 0\) — the total volume is exactly the sum of the volumes of the components.

4. The **intermolecular forces between unlike molecules are the same as those between like molecules**. If A and B are the two components, the A-B interaction must equal the A-A and B-B interactions.

The fourth condition is the cause of the other three. Benzene with toluene, and n-hexane with n-heptane, come close to ideal because their molecules are so similar.

stem: Write one example of each of ionisation, linkage and hydrated isomerism.
solution:
All three are kinds of **structural isomerism** in coordination compounds.

**1. Ionisation isomerism.** Two compounds have the same formula but exchange a ligand inside the coordination sphere with the counter ion outside it, so they give **different ions in solution**.

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5Br]SO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5SO_4]Br}\)

The first gives a precipitate with barium chloride, because the sulfate is free; the second gives a precipitate with silver nitrate instead, because the bromide is free.

**2. Linkage isomerism.** An **ambidentate** ligand attaches to the metal through one or the other of its two different donor atoms.

\(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(NO_2)]Cl_2}\) (bonded through nitrogen, the nitro form, yellow)

and \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5(ONO)]Cl_2}\) (bonded through oxygen, the nitrito form, red)

**3. Hydrate isomerism.** The isomers differ in how many water molecules are **inside** the coordination sphere as ligands and how many are outside as water of crystallisation.

\(\mathrm{[Cr(H_2O)_6]Cl_3}\) (violet)

\(\mathrm{[Cr(H_2O)_5Cl]Cl_2 \cdot H_2O}\) (blue green)

\(\mathrm{[Cr(H_2O)_4Cl_2]Cl \cdot 2H_2O}\) (dark green)

All three have the composition \(\mathrm{CrCl_3 \cdot 6H_2O}\), and they are distinguished by how much chloride silver nitrate precipitates from each.

stem:
Calculate the standard enthalpy of the reaction :

\(\mathrm{SiO_{2(s)} + 3C_{(graphite)} \rightarrow SiC_{(s)} + 2CO_{(g)}}\) from the following reactions :

(i) \(\mathrm{Si_{(s)} + O_{2(g)} \rightarrow SiO_{2(s)}}\), \(\Delta_r H^{\circ} = -911\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

(ii) \(\mathrm{2C_{(graphite)} + O_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2CO_{(g)}}\), \(\Delta_r H^{\circ} = -221\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

(iii) \(\mathrm{Si_{(s)} + C_{(graphite)} \rightarrow SiC_{(s)}}\), \(\Delta_r H^{\circ} = -65.3\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
solution:
Apply **Hess's law**: combine the three given equations so that they add up to the target, and combine their enthalpies the same way.

**Decide what each equation must do.**

- \(\mathrm{SiO_2}\) is a **reactant** in the target but a **product** in (i), so **reverse (i)** and change the sign of its enthalpy.
- \(\mathrm{2CO}\) is a product in the target and in (ii), so **keep (ii)** as it is.
- \(\mathrm{SiC}\) is a product in the target and in (iii), so **keep (iii)** as it is.

**Write them out.**

reversed (i): \(\mathrm{SiO_{2(s)} \rightarrow Si_{(s)} + O_{2(g)}}\), \(\Delta H = +911\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

(ii): \(\mathrm{2C_{(graphite)} + O_{2(g)} \rightarrow 2CO_{(g)}}\), \(\Delta H = -221\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

(iii): \(\mathrm{Si_{(s)} + C_{(graphite)} \rightarrow SiC_{(s)}}\), \(\Delta H = -65.3\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

**Add them.** On the left: \(\mathrm{SiO_2 + 2C + O_2 + Si + C}\). On the right: \(\mathrm{Si + O_2 + 2CO + SiC}\).

Cancelling the \(\mathrm{Si}\) and the \(\mathrm{O_2}\) that appear on both sides leaves

\(\mathrm{SiO_{2(s)} + 3C_{(graphite)} \rightarrow SiC_{(s)} + 2CO_{(g)}}\)

which is exactly the target.

**Add the enthalpies.**

\(\Delta_r H^{\circ} = (+911) + (-221) + (-65.3)\)

\(\therefore \Delta_r H^{\circ} = +624.7\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

The reaction is strongly **endothermic**, which is why silicon carbide is made in an electric furnace at very high temperature.

stem: Derive Ostwald's dilution law for weak acid. Obtain relation between solubility product and its solubility for \(\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}\).
solution:
**Part 1 — Ostwald's dilution law.**

For a weak monobasic acid HA of concentration \(c\) ionising to a degree \(\alpha\):

\(\mathrm{HA \rightleftharpoons H^{+} + A^{-}}\)

| | HA | \(\mathrm{H^{+}}\) | \(\mathrm{A^{-}}\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| initial | \(c\) | 0 | 0 |
| equilibrium | \(c(1-\alpha)\) | \(c\alpha\) | \(c\alpha\) |

\(K_a = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H^{+}}][\mathrm{A^{-}}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]} = \dfrac{(c\alpha)(c\alpha)}{c(1-\alpha)}\)

\(K_a = \dfrac{c\alpha^{2}}{1 - \alpha}\)

For a weak acid \(\alpha \ll 1\), so \(1 - \alpha \approx 1\):

\(K_a = c\alpha^{2}\)

\(\therefore \alpha = \sqrt{\dfrac{K_a}{c}}\)

The degree of dissociation increases as the solution is diluted.

**Part 2 — \(K_{sp}\) and solubility for \(\mathrm{Al(OH)_3}\).**

Let the solubility be \(s\ \mathrm{mol\ dm^{-3}}\). One formula unit gives one aluminium ion and **three** hydroxide ions:

\(\mathrm{Al(OH)_{3(s)} \rightleftharpoons Al^{3+}_{(aq)} + 3OH^{-}_{(aq)}}\)

So at saturation \([\mathrm{Al^{3+}}] = s\) and \([\mathrm{OH^{-}}] = 3s\).

\(K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Al^{3+}}][\mathrm{OH^{-}}]^{3}\)

\(K_{sp} = (s)(3s)^{3}\)

\(K_{sp} = s \times 27s^{3}\)

\(\therefore K_{sp} = 27s^{4}\)

or, solved for the solubility,

\(s = \sqrt[4]{\dfrac{K_{sp}}{27}}\)

The coefficient 3 must be used **twice** — once as a multiplier of \(s\) and once as a power — and forgetting either is the usual error.

stem:
60% of the reactant decomposes in 45 minutes in a first order reaction. Calculate the half life period of the reaction.

Write the relation between half life period and initial concentration for zero order reaction.
solution:
**Step 1 — find the rate constant.** For a first order reaction,

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{t}\log\dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]_t}\)

If 60% decomposes, **40% remains**, so take \([A]_0 = 100\) and \([A]_t = 40\):

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{45}\log\dfrac{100}{40}\)

\(k = \dfrac{2.303}{45} \times \log 2.5\)

\(k = 0.05118 \times 0.3979\)

\(k = 0.02036\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}\)

**Step 2 — the half life.** For a first order reaction,

\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.02036}\)

\(\therefore t_{1/2} = 34.04\ \mathrm{minutes}\)

**Relation for a zero order reaction.** Putting \([A]_t = \dfrac{[A]_0}{2}\) into \(kt = [A]_0 - [A]_t\),

\(k\,t_{1/2} = [A]_0 - \dfrac{[A]_0}{2} = \dfrac{[A]_0}{2}\)

\(\therefore t_{1/2} = \dfrac{[A]_0}{2k}\)

So for a zero order reaction the half life is **directly proportional to the initial concentration** — in sharp contrast to a first order reaction, whose half life does not depend on it at all.

stem:
Write the conditions of colour of transition metal ion.

Write the alloy used in Fischer Tropsch process.
solution:
**Conditions for a transition metal ion to be coloured.**

1. **The ion must have a partly filled \(d\) subshell.** There must be at least one \(d\) electron to promote and at least one vacancy for it to move into. An ion with \(d^{0}\) or \(d^{10}\) has neither, so \(\mathrm{Sc^{3+}}\) and \(\mathrm{Zn^{2+}}\) are colourless.

2. **The \(d\) orbitals must be split into two energy levels** by the surrounding ligands, in solution, or by the neighbouring ions in the crystal lattice. Without a ligand field the five \(d\) orbitals stay degenerate and no transition is possible.

3. **The energy gap must correspond to a wavelength in the visible region**, so that visible light is absorbed. The colour seen is the **complement** of the colour absorbed.

When all three hold, an electron absorbs a photon and jumps from the lower set of \(d\) orbitals to the higher one — a **\(d\)-\(d\) transition** — and the ion appears coloured.

**Alloy used in the Fischer-Tropsch process.**

The **cobalt-thorium** catalyst, cobalt with thoria supported on kieselguhr. Iron based catalysts are also used industrially.

The process converts synthesis gas, a mixture of carbon monoxide and hydrogen, into liquid hydrocarbon fuels:

\(\mathrm{nCO + (2n+1)H_2 \longrightarrow C_nH_{2n+2} + nH_2O}\)

stem: Explain anomalous behaviour of oxygen with respect to atomicity, magnetic property and oxidation state.
solution:
Oxygen is the first member of group 16 and differs from sulfur, selenium and tellurium because it is very small, highly electronegative, and has **no vacant \(d\) orbitals**.

**Atomicity.** Oxygen is **diatomic**, existing as \(\mathrm{O_2}\) molecules held by a double bond. The others are **polyatomic**: sulfur forms \(\mathrm{S_8}\) puckered rings, and selenium and tellurium form long chains.

The reason is size. Oxygen is small enough to form strong \(p\pi{-}p\pi\) multiple bonds with itself, so two atoms satisfy each other completely. The larger atoms cannot overlap their \(p\) orbitals sideways well enough for a \(\pi\) bond, so they form single bonds to several neighbours instead.

**Magnetic property.** \(\mathrm{O_2}\) is **paramagnetic**, while the other elements in their normal forms are diamagnetic.

Molecular orbital theory explains it: the last two electrons of \(\mathrm{O_2}\) occupy two degenerate antibonding \(\pi^{*}\) orbitals singly with parallel spins, leaving **two unpaired electrons**. This is the classic result that valence bond theory, which pairs them into a double bond, cannot account for.

**Oxidation state.** Oxygen shows a maximum of \(-2\) and does not exhibit the \(+4\) and \(+6\) states common for sulfur, selenium and tellurium.

The cause is the absence of \(d\) orbitals: oxygen cannot unpair and promote electrons to expand its octet. It is also second only to fluorine in electronegativity, so positive oxidation states are unfavourable. Its only positive state is \(+2\), in \(\mathrm{OF_2}\), and only because fluorine is more electronegative still.

subtopic: Chemical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
stem: Explain cross Cannizzaro reaction.
solution:
**The cross Cannizzaro reaction** is a Cannizzaro reaction carried out between **two different** aldehydes, both lacking an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen, in concentrated alkali.

One is oxidised to the carboxylate and the other reduced to the alcohol, but unlike the ordinary Cannizzaro reaction the outcome is **not** a mixture of four products, because one of the two is a much better hydride donor.

**Example — benzaldehyde with formaldehyde.**

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO + HCHO + NaOH \longrightarrow C_6H_5CH_2OH + HCOONa}\)

The products are benzyl alcohol and sodium formate.

**Why it goes this way.** Formaldehyde is the best hydride donor of all aldehydes: its carbonyl carbon is the least hindered and carries no electron-releasing group, so hydroxide adds to it readily and the resulting intermediate gives up its hydride easily.

So **formaldehyde is always oxidised** to formate, and the other aldehyde is always **reduced** to the alcohol.

The synthetic value is exactly this predictability: adding excess formaldehyde converts another non-enolisable aldehyde cleanly to its alcohol, whereas a self-Cannizzaro would give only half the material as alcohol and half as acid.

stem: Draw structure of Zwitter ion of sulfanilic acid.
solution:
Sulfanilic acid is 4-aminobenzenesulfonic acid, \(\mathrm{H_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}SO_3H}\). It carries a **basic** amino group and a **strongly acidic** sulfonic acid group on the same benzene ring, at opposite ends.

The sulfonic acid is strong enough to protonate the amine internally, so the proton transfers from the \(\mathrm{{-}SO_3H}\) to the \(\mathrm{{-}NH_2}\):

\(\mathrm{{}^{+}H_3N{-}C_6H_4{-}SO_3^{-}}\)

The molecule carries a **positive charge on nitrogen and a negative charge on the sulfonate oxygen**, but is electrically **neutral overall**. This internal salt is the zwitter ion.

Its consequences are visible in the physical properties: sulfanilic acid has an unusually high melting point, decomposing rather than melting cleanly, is sparingly soluble in water and insoluble in organic solvents, and behaves like an ionic solid rather than a typical organic compound.

stem:
Identify A, B, C and rewrite the chemical reactions :

\(\mathrm{H_3C{-}CH_2Cl + KOH_{(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 'A' \xrightarrow{\text{hot Cu powder}} 'B'}\), and \(\mathrm{'B' \xrightarrow{K_2Cr_2O_7 / dil.\ H_2SO_4} 'C'}\)
solution:
**Step 1 — identify A.** Chloroethane with **aqueous** KOH undergoes nucleophilic substitution, the hydroxide displacing the chloride:

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2Cl + KOH_{(aq)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} CH_3CH_2OH + KCl}\)

\(\mathbf{A}\) is **ethanol**.

The word *aqueous* is doing the work here. With **alcoholic** KOH the reaction would be elimination instead, giving ethene.

**Step 2 — identify B.** Ethanol vapour passed over hot copper at about 573 K is dehydrogenated. A primary alcohol gives an aldehyde:

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2OH \xrightarrow[573\ K]{Cu} CH_3CHO + H_2\uparrow}\)

\(\mathbf{B}\) is **ethanal** (acetaldehyde).

**Step 3 — identify C.** Ethanal is oxidised by acidified potassium dichromate to the carboxylic acid:

\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO + [O] \xrightarrow{K_2Cr_2O_7 / dil.\ H_2SO_4} CH_3COOH}\)

\(\mathbf{C}\) is **ethanoic acid** (acetic acid).

\(\therefore\) A = ethanol, B = ethanal, C = ethanoic acid. The orange dichromate turning green is the visible sign of the last step.

stem: Explain optical isomerism in 2-chlorobutane.
solution:
2-chlorobutane is \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CHCl{-}CH_2{-}CH_3}\).

**The chiral centre.** Carbon 2 carries four **different** groups:

- \(\mathrm{{-}H}\)
- \(\mathrm{{-}Cl}\)
- \(\mathrm{{-}CH_3}\), a methyl group
- \(\mathrm{{-}C_2H_5}\), an ethyl group

A carbon bonded to four different groups is **asymmetric**, or chiral.

**Why that gives optical isomerism.** With a chiral centre the molecule has no plane of symmetry and no centre of symmetry, so it cannot be superimposed on its own mirror image. The two mirror images are distinct compounds called **enantiomers**, and interconverting them would need a bond to be broken.

The two enantiomers rotate the plane of plane-polarised light through **equal angles in opposite directions**, one dextrorotatory \((+)\) and the other laevorotatory \((-)\). They are identical in every other physical property.

Since there is one chiral carbon, the number of optical isomers is \(2^{1} = 2\).

**The racemic mixture.** An equimolar mixture of the two shows **no** rotation, the two effects cancelling exactly. It is optically inactive by **external compensation** — every molecule in it is still chiral.

For contrast, 1-chlorobutane has no carbon bearing four different groups and can never be optically active.

subtopic: Chemical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
stem: Write Clemmenson's reduction reaction of propanone. Write Fehling solution test for ethanal.
solution:
**Clemmensen reduction of propanone.** Zinc amalgam with concentrated hydrochloric acid reduces the carbonyl group all the way to a methylene group:

\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3 + 4[H] \xrightarrow{Zn{-}Hg\ /\ conc.\ HCl} CH_3CH_2CH_3 + H_2O}\)

The product is **propane**. The reduction does not stop at propan-2-ol; the carbon-oxygen bond is broken completely.

**Fehling solution test for ethanal.** Fehling's solution is a deep blue alkaline solution of a copper(II) tartrate complex, made by mixing Fehling A (aqueous \(\mathrm{CuSO_4}\)) with Fehling B (alkaline sodium potassium tartrate) just before use.

On warming with ethanal the aldehyde is oxidised to the carboxylate and copper(II) is reduced to copper(I):

\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO + 2Cu^{2+} + 5OH^{-} \longrightarrow CH_3COO^{-} + Cu_2O\downarrow + 3H_2O}\)

**Observation.** The blue colour of the solution fades and a **reddish brown precipitate of cuprous oxide**, \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\), separates.

**What it distinguishes.** Fehling's solution oxidises **aliphatic aldehydes** but not ketones, so propanone gives no reaction. Aromatic aldehydes such as benzaldehyde also fail the test, which is how it distinguishes them from aliphatic ones.

stem: How is dioxygen prepared in laboratory from \(\mathrm{KClO_3}\)?
solution:
Dioxygen is prepared in the laboratory by heating potassium chlorate in the presence of manganese dioxide as catalyst:

\(\mathrm{2KClO_{3(s)} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{MnO_2} 2KCl_{(s)} + 3O_{2(g)}}\)

**Procedure.** A mixture of potassium chlorate with a small quantity of manganese dioxide is heated in a hard glass test tube fitted with a delivery tube. The oxygen evolved is collected **over water** by downward displacement, since oxygen is only sparingly soluble in water.

**Role of \(\mathrm{MnO_2}\).** It is a catalyst, lowering the decomposition temperature from about 670 K to roughly 520 K. It is not consumed and can be recovered unchanged at the end, which is how it is shown to be catalytic rather than a reactant.

stem:
Write the chemical reaction to convert :

(a) phenol to benzoquinone

(b) phenol to cyclohexanol
solution:
**(a) Phenol to benzoquinone — oxidation.** Sodium dichromate in sulfuric acid, or chromic acid:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH \xrightarrow{Na_2Cr_2O_7 / H_2SO_4} C_6H_4O_2 + H_2O}\)

The product is **p-benzoquinone**, cyclohexa-2,5-diene-1,4-dione. The ring **loses its aromaticity**: the hydroxyl oxygen becomes one carbonyl group and a second carbonyl appears at the para position, leaving two isolated double bonds in the ring.

**(b) Phenol to cyclohexanol — reduction of the ring.** Hydrogen over a nickel catalyst at 433 K:

\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH + 3H_2 \xrightarrow[433\ K]{Ni} C_6H_{11}OH}\)

Three molecules of hydrogen are needed, one for each double bond of the benzene ring. The hydroxyl group is **not** touched: catalytic hydrogenation saturates the ring but leaves the \(\mathrm{C{-}OH}\) bond intact.

The pair is a useful contrast — the same starting material, oxidised in one case and reduced in the other, with the ring destroyed aromatically in both but in opposite directions.

subtopic: Enthalpy and Enthalpies of Physical Transformations
stem:
Define :

(a) Standard enthalpy of combustion.

(b) Enthalpy of atomization.
solution:
**(a) Standard enthalpy of combustion.** The enthalpy change when **one mole** of a substance is completely burnt in an excess of oxygen, with all reactants and products in their standard states at a specified temperature, usually 298 K.

It is written \(\Delta_c H^{\circ}\) and is **always negative**, combustion being exothermic. For methane:

\(\mathrm{CH_{4(g)} + 2O_{2(g)} \longrightarrow CO_{2(g)} + 2H_2O_{(l)}}\), \(\Delta_c H^{\circ} = -890\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

Both **one mole** and **completely** are load-bearing: complete combustion of a hydrocarbon means the carbon must finish as \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), not as CO.

**(b) Enthalpy of atomization.** The enthalpy change when **one mole** of a substance is completely dissociated into its **gaseous atoms** under standard conditions.

It is written \(\Delta_a H^{\circ}\) and is always **positive**, since energy must be supplied to break bonds.

\(\mathrm{H_{2(g)} \longrightarrow 2H_{(g)}}\), \(\Delta_a H^{\circ} = +435\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

\(\mathrm{Na_{(s)} \longrightarrow Na_{(g)}}\), \(\Delta_a H^{\circ} = +108\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

For a diatomic molecule the enthalpy of atomisation is equal to its bond dissociation enthalpy.

stem: Draw the structure of D-ribose sugar.
solution:
D-ribose is an **aldopentose**: a five-carbon sugar with an aldehyde group at \(\mathrm{C_1}\).

**Open chain (Fischer) structure.**

\(\mathrm{CHO{-}CHOH{-}CHOH{-}CHOH{-}CH_2OH}\)

In the Fischer projection all three hydroxyl groups, on \(\mathrm{C_2}\), \(\mathrm{C_3}\) and \(\mathrm{C_4}\), point to the **right**. It is designated **D** because the hydroxyl on the chiral carbon furthest from the carbonyl, \(\mathrm{C_4}\), is on the right.

**Cyclic (furanose) form.** In solution ribose exists mainly as a five-membered ring, formed when the \(\mathrm{C_4}\) hydroxyl adds across the \(\mathrm{C_1}\) aldehyde:

the ring contains \(\mathrm{C_1}\), \(\mathrm{C_2}\), \(\mathrm{C_3}\), \(\mathrm{C_4}\) and one oxygen, with \(\mathrm{{-}OH}\) groups on \(\mathrm{C_1}\), \(\mathrm{C_2}\) and \(\mathrm{C_3}\) and a \(\mathrm{{-}CH_2OH}\) group on \(\mathrm{C_4}\).

This furanose form is the one present in RNA. In DNA the \(\mathrm{C_2}\) hydroxyl is absent, giving 2-deoxy-D-ribose.

stem: Write the uses of bronze alloy.
solution:
Bronze is an alloy of **copper with tin**, typically about 88% copper and 12% tin.

**Uses.**

1. **Statues, medals and coins**, because it casts well, takes fine detail and weathers to a stable protective patina.
2. **Bearings, bushes and gears**, since it is hard, has a low coefficient of friction and resists wear.
3. **Ship propellers and marine fittings**, being highly resistant to corrosion by sea water.
4. **Bells and cymbals** — bell metal is a bronze with a higher tin content, around 22%, which gives it its resonance.
5. **Springs and electrical contacts**, in the form of phosphor bronze.

Bronze is harder and more corrosion resistant than either copper or tin alone, which is the general reason alloys are made.

stem: Distinguish between order and molecularity of a reaction.
solution:
| Order of reaction | Molecularity of reaction |
|---|---|
| The sum of the powers of the concentration terms in the experimentally determined rate law. | The number of reactant species that collide simultaneously in an elementary reaction. |
| Determined **experimentally**. | Deduced **theoretically** from the mechanism. |
| May be zero, fractional or whole. | Always a whole number; never zero or fractional. |
| Applies to the overall reaction, however many steps. | Defined only for a **single elementary step**. |
| Can change with conditions — pseudo-first order, for example. | Fixed for a given step. |
| No upper limit in principle. | Rarely exceeds 3. |

**The link.** For an elementary reaction, and only then, the order equals the molecularity. For a multi-step reaction the order is set by the **slowest step**, so it need have no relation to the coefficients of the overall balanced equation.

stem: Write gases liberated at cathode and anode during electrolysis of aqueous NaCl solution.
solution:
**At the cathode — hydrogen.**

\(\mathrm{2H_2O + 2e^{-} \longrightarrow H_{2(g)}\uparrow + 2OH^{-}}\)

Water is reduced in preference to \(\mathrm{Na^{+}}\), because the reduction potential of water \((-0.83\ \mathrm{V})\) is far higher than that of sodium \((-2.71\ \mathrm{V})\). This is why sodium metal cannot be obtained from an aqueous solution and must be extracted from molten NaCl.

**At the anode — chlorine.**

\(\mathrm{2Cl^{-} \longrightarrow Cl_{2(g)}\uparrow + 2e^{-}}\)

On thermodynamic grounds alone water should be oxidised to oxygen in preference to chloride, but chlorine is obtained because the oxidation of water has a high **overpotential** on the electrode surface, which makes it kinetically slow.

**Net result.** Hydrogen at the cathode, chlorine at the anode, and sodium hydroxide accumulating in the solution. This is the **chlor-alkali process**, the industrial source of all three products.

stem: Write two uses of neon.
solution:
**1. Neon signs and fluorescent lamps.** Neon at low pressure in a discharge tube emits a characteristic bright **reddish orange** glow when a high voltage is applied. Mixing it with other gases or coating the tube gives other colours. It is also used in beacon lamps at airfields and for warning signals, because the light penetrates fog and mist better than ordinary light.

**2. In high voltage indicators and lightning arresters**, and in television tubes and voltage stabilisers, where its low ionisation potential and inertness are useful.

(Also accepted: liquid neon as a cryogenic refrigerant, having a greater refrigerating capacity per unit volume than liquid helium; and in growing plants in gas-filled greenhouses.)

stem:
When gold crystallizes, it forms face-centred cubic cell. The unit cell edge length is 408 pm. Calculate the density of gold.

[Molar mass of gold = \(197\ \mathrm{g\ mole^{-1}}\)]
solution:
\(\rho = \dfrac{nM}{a^{3}N_A}\)

**Step 1 — atoms per unit cell.** For face centred cubic, \(n = 4\).

**Step 2 — convert the edge length to centimetres.**

\(a = 408\ \mathrm{pm} = 408 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{cm} = 4.08 \times 10^{-8}\ \mathrm{cm}\)

\(a^{3} = (4.08 \times 10^{-8})^{3} = 67.92 \times 10^{-24} = 6.792 \times 10^{-23}\ \mathrm{cm^{3}}\)

**Step 3 — substitute.**

\(\rho = \dfrac{4 \times 197}{6.792 \times 10^{-23} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}}\)

\(\rho = \dfrac{788}{6.792 \times 6.022}\)

\(\rho = \dfrac{788}{40.90}\)

\(\therefore \rho = 19.27\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}}\)

This agrees closely with the measured density of gold, \(19.3\ \mathrm{g\ cm^{-3}}\).

stem: Which flower is an example of self cleaning?
solution:
The **lotus** flower.

Its leaves and petals are covered with nanoscale waxy bumps, so a water droplet cannot spread and sits almost spherically on the surface, with a contact angle above 150 degrees. As the droplet rolls off it picks up dust and dirt particles and carries them away, leaving the surface clean.

This is called the **lotus effect**, or superhydrophobicity. It is the model for self-cleaning paints, glass and fabrics, which reproduce the same nanostructured surface artificially.

**Write the monomer used for preparation of PVC.**

The monomer is **vinyl chloride**, \(\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCl}\), which polymerises by addition:

\(n\,\mathrm{CH_2{=}CHCl \longrightarrow (\!-CH_2{-}CHCl-\!)_n}\)

stem:
Explain the formation of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) ion on the basis of Valence bond theory.

Convert the following :

(a) acetic acid to ethyl acetate

(b) acetic acid to ethyl alcohol.
solution:
**Formation of \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+}}\) on valence bond theory.**

**Step 1 — oxidation state and configuration.** The ammonia ligands are neutral and the ion carries \(3+\), so cobalt is \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\).

Cobalt is \(\mathrm{[Ar]\,3d^{7}4s^{2}}\); removing three electrons gives

\(\mathrm{Co^{3+}: [Ar]\ 3d^{6}}\)

**Step 2 — effect of the ligand.** Ammonia is a **strong field** ligand. It forces the six \(3d\) electrons to pair up into three of the five \(d\) orbitals:

\(t_{2g}^{6}\), leaving **two \(3d\) orbitals empty**

**Step 3 — hybridisation.** Those two vacant inner \(3d\) orbitals, together with the \(4s\) and the three \(4p\) orbitals, hybridise:

\(d^{2}sp^{3}\)

Six such hybrid orbitals point to the corners of a regular **octahedron**, and each accepts a lone pair from one ammonia molecule, forming six coordinate bonds.

**Step 4 — properties that follow.**

- Geometry: **octahedral**
- Since inner \(3d\) orbitals are used, it is an **inner orbital** or **low spin** complex
- Unpaired electrons: **zero**, so the ion is **diamagnetic**, \(\mu = 0\ \mathrm{BM}\)

The contrast with \(\mathrm{[CoF_6]^{3-}}\) is the point: fluoride is a weak field ligand, cannot force pairing, so the same \(\mathrm{Co^{3+}}\) uses outer \(4d\) orbitals, is \(sp^{3}d^{2}\), and is paramagnetic with four unpaired electrons.

**Conversions.**

**(a) Acetic acid to ethyl acetate — esterification.** Heat with ethanol and a little concentrated sulfuric acid:

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH + C_2H_5OH \xrightleftharpoons[\Delta]{conc.\ H_2SO_4} CH_3COOC_2H_5 + H_2O}\)

The reaction is reversible; the sulfuric acid both catalyses it and removes the water, driving the equilibrium forward.

**(b) Acetic acid to ethyl alcohol — reduction.**

\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH \xrightarrow[(ii)\ H_3O^{+}]{(i)\ LiAlH_4} CH_3CH_2OH}\)

Lithium aluminium hydride is needed because the carboxyl group resists reduction: its carbonyl carbon is already stabilised by the hydroxyl oxygen, so \(\mathrm{NaBH_4}\) will not touch it.
